claims.claim: Every tenant has a single OneLake, built on ADLS, storing tables in Delta Parquet or Iceberg; you cannot create multiple OneLakes.

OneLake URI formats by name and by GUID; GUIDs do not change on rename; abfs URIs do not allow special characters such as spaces in the workspace name; the global endpoint may route data out of region, and regional endpoints avoid this.

concept_html:
Every Fabric tenant has exactly one OneLake. You cannot create a second one or delete it. It is built on Azure Data Lake Storage and stores tables in open formats: Delta Parquet or Iceberg. Every Fabric engine (Spark, the SQL engines, Power BI's Direct Lake, KQL) reads the same files, so one copy of the data serves them all.

OneLake mirrors the Fabric hierarchy: a folder per workspace, and inside it a folder per item, named with its type. A lakehouse holds two areas: Tables for managed Delta tables and Files for anything else.

You address data with an ADLS-style path:

https://onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/<workspace>/<item>.<itemtype>/<path>
abfss://<workspace>@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/<item>.<itemtype>/<path>

For example abfss://sales_prod@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/lh_sales.lakehouse/Tables/orders. The item type is lower case: .lakehouse, .warehouse.

Names change. GUIDs do not. OneLake accepts the workspace and item GUIDs in place of names, and they stay fixed when someone renames the workspace or item. With GUIDs you give both the workspace and the item as GUIDs, and you drop the item type. You find them in the item's URL in the Fabric portal.

Use GUIDs in pipelines, jobs and code that other people will run. Two more reasons from Microsoft Learn:

  • The abfs driver URI does not allow special characters such as spaces in the workspace name. GUIDs avoid the problem.
  • The global endpoint onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com can route through another region. If data residency matters, use your workspace's regional endpoint, https://<region>-onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com.

Because tools that speak ADLS APIs can read OneLake, Azure Databricks, Azure Storage Explorer or Python's Azure SDK can read Fabric data with the right permissions.

exercises.prompt_html:
Write onelake_path(workspace: str, item: str, item_type: str, relative: str) -> str returning abfss://<workspace>@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/<item>.<item_type>/<relative>.

  • item_type must be "lakehouse" or "warehouse". Otherwise raise ValueError.
  • Raise ValueError if workspace or item contains a space.
  • Strip leading slashes from relative.
exercises.solution:
ONELAKE_HOST = "onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com"
ITEM_TYPES = frozenset({"lakehouse", "warehouse"})


def onelake_path(workspace: str, item: str, item_type: str, relative: str) -> str:
    """abfss path to data in a OneLake item, addressed by name.

    Args:
        workspace: Workspace name, without spaces.
        item: Item name, without spaces.
        item_type: "lakehouse" or "warehouse".
        relative: Path inside the item, such as Tables/orders.

    Returns:
        The abfss URI.

    Raises:
        ValueError: For an unknown item type or names with spaces.
    """
    if item_type not in ITEM_TYPES:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported item type: {item_type!r}")
    if " " in workspace or " " in item:
        raise ValueError("abfs URIs do not allow spaces; use GUIDs instead")
    return f"abfss://{workspace}@{ONELAKE_HOST}/{item}.{item_type}/{relative.lstrip('/')}"

title: OneLake, one lake per tenant
why_html: A Databricks job read a Fabric lakehouse through abfss://Sales Analytics@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/.... It failed on the first run, because the workspace name held a space. The engineer renamed the workspace to SalesAnalytics. The job worked, and four Power BI dataflows and two pipelines that referred to the old name broke that night. Using the workspace and item GUIDs would have avoided both failures.
